1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: Male patient, 68 years old, farmer, was emergently admitted on Day 0 due to "fever, cough, sputum production for 2 weeks, dyspnea, inability to lie flat for 3 days." Before symptom onset, the patient developed fever, cough, and sputum production after alcohol intoxication, vomiting, and exposure to cold. Body temperature fluctuated between 38.5°-39.5°, accompanied by chills. He self-administered cefixime capsules and Asmeton, with poor effect. Chest CT at a local hospital showed a mass-like area of increased density in the left upper lobe and a small pleural effusion. Left upper lobe pneumonia was considered, and he was given anti-infective, antiasthmatic, and expectorant treatment for 1 week. Symptoms were relieved, but 2 days before admission he developed persistent high fever, dyspnea, and decreased blood pressure (80/50 mmHg). Previous physical examinations were unremarkable. He denied a history of contact with infectious diseases and drug allergy history. Physical examination on admission: T: 39.5°, P: 140 beats/min, R: 46 breaths/min, BP: 80/50 mmHg. He was conscious, appeared acutely ill, had cyanosis of the lips and fingers, cold clammy skin with profuse sweating over the whole body, no jaundice, no petechiae, rash, or ecchymosis, no enlarged superficial lymph nodes, bilateral pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Neck was supple, no jugular venous distention, trachea midline, thyroid not enlarged, thorax symmetrical without deformity, dullness to percussion over the left lung, decreased breath sounds in the left lung, medium and fine moist rales audible, coarse breath sounds in the right lung, heart rate 140 beats/min, regular rhythm, no murmur heard in any valve auscultation area. No positive abdominal or cardiac findings, bilateral knee tendon reflexes present, Babinski sign negative. Ancillary examinations: Arterial blood gas analysis: (oxygen inhalation 3 L/min) pH: 7.28, PaCO2: 33 mmHg, PaO2: 47 mmHg, HCO3-: 15.2 mmol/L, SaO2: 75%. Complete blood count: WBC: 14.85*109/L, neutrophils: 89.9%, lymphocytes: 4.1%, platelets: 266*109/L. Biochemistry: sodium: 133 mmol/L, glucose: 10.1 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen: 9.3 mmol/L, total bilirubin: 57.9 umol/L, direct bilirubin: 36.8 umol/L, indirect bilirubin: 21.1 umol/L, total protein: 58.2 g/L, albumin: 26 g/L, glutamyl aminotransferase: 71.4 U/L, cholinesterase: 2072 U/L, C-reactive protein: 105 mg/L, interleukin-6: 502 pg/ml. Myocardial enzyme panel: myoglobin: 71.5 ug/L, lactate dehydrogenase: 47 U/L. ESR: 88 mm/h. Coagulation panel: prothrombin time: 12.7 s, fibrinogen: 6.55 g/L, D-dimer: 9426 ug/ml. ECG: sinus tachycardia: 140 beats/min, normal electrical axis. Bedside chest X-ray: patchy flocculent opacity in the left upper lung, large dense opacity in the middle and lower lung fields, with an air-fluid level within it, blunting of the left costophrenic angle, disordered hilar structures in both lungs, cardiac silhouette not clearly visualized. Chest CT: bilateral pulmonary infection, left lower lobe consolidation, abscess (with internal fluid level), left loculated pleural effusion. Chest ultrasonography: large left pleural effusion, small right pleural effusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Aspiration pneumonia with lung abscess, sepsis/septic shock
supporting_evidence: Before onset, there was a history of "alcohol intoxication, vomiting, and exposure to cold," consistent with a high-risk background for aspiration.
Fever, cough, and sputum production for 2 weeks, followed later by dyspnea and inability to lie flat, suggesting progression of severe pulmonary infection
Temperature 39.5°, WBC 14.85*10^9/L, neutrophils 89.9%, CRP 105mg/L, IL-6 502pg/ml, ESR 88mm/h, supporting severe bacterial infection

Chest X-ray showed patchy flocculent opacity in the left upper lung and a large dense opacity in the middle and lower lung fields, with an air-fluid level within; chest CT showed left lower lobe consolidation and abscess (with an internal fluid level), consistent with lung abscess

Dullness to percussion over the left lung, decreased breath sounds in the left lung, with audible medium and fine moist rales; chest ultrasound showed a large left pleural effusion, suggesting infection involving the pleura

On admission, BP was 80/50 mmHg, P was 140 beats/min, the skin was cold, clammy, and diaphoretic; arterial blood gas showed PaO2 47 mmHg, pH 7.28, and HCO3- 15.2 mmol/L, consistent with severe infection accompanied by shock and hypoxemia.
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia
supporting_evidence: High fever, cough, and sputum production persisted for 2 weeks, and after anti-infective treatment at a local hospital there was brief improvement followed by recurrent persistent high fever, suggesting bacterial pneumonia with strong invasiveness or poor treatment response.
Both chest X-ray and CT showed intrapulmonary consolidation and an air-fluid level/abscess, consistent with the imaging features of pulmonary tissue necrosis and cavitation formation.
Loculated left pleural effusion and massive left pleural effusion may be manifestations of severe necrotizing pneumonia complicated by pleural infection.
Markedly elevated infection markers accompanied by hypotension and severe hypoxemia, suggesting fulminant severe pulmonary infection
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide clear etiologic evidence to support a specific necrotizing pathogen.

The lesions are predominantly left lower lobe consolidation and abscess; although this supports severe infection, it cannot be completely distinguished from a simple lung abscess based on the first-stage information alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Complicated parapneumonic pleural effusion/empyema
supporting_evidence: Chest CT at the local hospital had already shown a small pleural effusion; subsequent chest CT indicated a loculated left pleural effusion; chest ultrasonography showed a large left pleural effusion and a small right pleural effusion, suggesting rapid progression of the pleural effusion.
On physical examination, dullness to percussion over the left lung and decreased breath sounds in the left lung, consistent with signs of a large pleural effusion
Persistent high fever and markedly elevated white blood cell count and inflammatory markers support the possibility of an infectious pleural effusion or even empyema.
The presence of a pulmonary abscess and severe pneumonia is a high-risk background for developing empyema.
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 information did not provide the characteristics, biochemical results, or bacteriological results of the pleural puncture fluid, so empyema cannot yet be directly confirmed.
Imaging has already shown definite pulmonary consolidation and abscess, and part of the dyspnea can also be explained by the pulmonary consolidation itself.

differential_diagnoses.name: Postobstructive pneumonia/lung abscess secondary to lung cancer
supporting_evidence: The patient is a 68-year-old male, in the high-incidence age group for lung cancer.
A chest CT at a local hospital previously described a "mass-like area of increased density in the left upper lobe"; post-obstructive infection caused by a neoplastic lesion should be considered.
After anti-infective treatment, sustained improvement was not achieved, and the condition deteriorated rapidly, suggesting a possible underlying obstructive lesion.
Imaging shows severe focal lesions and pleural effusion; in elderly patients, vigilance is warranted for tumor-related secondary infection.
opposing_evidence: This chest radiograph and chest CT more prominently showed bilateral pulmonary infection, left lower lobe consolidation, abscess, and pleural effusion, with stronger evidence of acute infection.
The stage 1 information did not provide tumor-supporting information such as smoking history, weight loss, long-term hemoptysis, or definite hilar/mediastinal enlargement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis with secondary infection or tuberculous empyema
supporting_evidence: Fever, cough with sputum production, and pleural effusion are present; pulmonary TB can have similar manifestations.
The left upper lobe was previously described early on as a mass-like area of increased density; TB should be considered in the differential diagnosis of the upper lobe lesion.
ESR 88mm/h is markedly elevated and can be seen in chronic infections such as TB
opposing_evidence: The course is relatively acute, and is characterized mainly by persistent high fever, shock, and marked neutrophilia, which more strongly supports acute bacterial infection.
Imaging suggests a lung abscess with an air-fluid level, severe consolidation, and loculated pleural effusion, more consistent with pyogenic infection.
The first-stage information states denial of a history of exposure to infectious diseases.

stage2_input.text: Thoracoscopy showed a large amount of yellow pus in the left pleural cavity. After suction, a large amount of purulent exudate adherent to both the visceral and parietal pleura was seen. After dividing the adhesions and clearing the purulent exudate using electrocautery and biopsy forceps, pleural hyperemia, edema, and erosion were seen. Multiple biopsies of the visceral pleura were obtained; the pathology report showed a large amount of neutrophilic infiltration and necrosis, followed by copious normal saline irrigation.

images.near_text: Aspirate pus, remove purulent slough, and debride necrotic tissue.
A large amount of pus and purulent coating adherent, with unclear pleural cavity structures
B Pleural congestion, edema, erosion, thickening, with adherent purulent exudate
A Pleural congestion, edema, erosion, and thickening, with adherent purulent coating

differential_diagnoses.name: TB, tumor
exclusion_reasons: Observe the characteristics of pleural lesions under endoscopy (hyperemia, edema, erosion), combined with multipoint biopsy to obtain pathologic evidence

5.updated_differential_diagnoses.name: TB, tumor
evidence: Persistent fever and refractory shock despite continued conventional anti-infective therapy and drainage
exclusion_reasons: Observe the characteristics of pleural lesions under endoscopy (hyperemia, edema, erosion), combined with multipoint biopsy to obtain pathologic evidence

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Through sputum testing, metagenomic sequencing (NGS), and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, Staphylococcus aureus was rapidly identified as the pathogen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 68-year-old man who developed fever, cough, and sputum production for 2 weeks after vomiting while intoxicated, followed by progression to dyspnea and orthopnea, and at admission had a high fever of 39.5℃, hypotension, severe hypoxemia, and manifestations of septic shock; chest radiograph and CT suggested severe pulmonary infection, left lower lobe consolidation, lung abscess with an air-fluid level, and loculated pleural effusion/empyema. The condition was critical and empiric anti-infective treatment at the local hospital was ineffective, so lower respiratory tract microbiologic clues had to be obtained as soon as possible. Sputum testing can directly identify pathogenic bacteria from respiratory secretions, helping determine whether this episode of severe pneumonia and secondary empyema is caused by bacterial infection, and providing a basis for subsequent molecular testing and antimicrobial susceptibility results. The clinical goal of this test is to identify the pulmonary infectious pathogen as quickly as possible, support the diagnosis of pyogenic bacterial pneumonia, and reduce the uncertainty of differentiating among aspiration pneumonia, necrotizing pneumonia, TB, or tumor with secondary infection based on imaging alone, thereby guiding timely, targeted anti-infective therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Through sputum testing, metagenomic sequencing (NGS), and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, Staphylococcus aureus was rapidly identified as the pathogen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's condition is progressing rapidly and has already developed lung abscess, empyema, respiratory failure, infectious shock, and a risk of MODS, consistent with a critical pulmonary infection in which the pathogen needs to be identified as soon as possible. After previously receiving conventional anti-infective treatment at a local hospital, there was only transient improvement, followed by recurrent persistent high fever and rapid deterioration, suggesting that routine empiric therapy did not provide effective coverage or that the pathogen is highly invasive. Imaging showed intrapulmonary necrosis, an air-fluid level, and pleural involvement. In the differential diagnosis, in addition to common bacteria, anaerobic bacteria, TB, fungi, and secondary infection of a tumor also need to be distinguished. NGS can identify pathogens in respiratory specimens more rapidly and broadly when traditional culture results are still pending or the positive rate is limited, helping to quickly identify the true causative pathogen in the setting of complex critical illness. This test is intended to address the key question of "which pathogen is causing severe necrotizing pneumonia with empyema," helping to confirm Staphylococcus aureus infection as early as possible, narrow the differential diagnosis, and support a shift in the treatment plan from empiric coverage to more targeted antimicrobial decision-making.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Through sputum testing, metagenomic sequencing (NGS), and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, Staphylococcus aureus was rapidly identified as the pathogen.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At the time of admission, this patient was already in critical condition, with persistent high fever, marked elevation of the white blood cell count and inflammatory markers, hypotension, severe hypoxemia, and a tendency toward multiorgan injury; in addition, prior empiric treatment with cefixime and other agents had been ineffective, indicating that identifying only the name of the pathogen was still insufficient to ensure treatment success. Staphylococcus aureus has clinically significant differences in resistance patterns, and it is particularly necessary to determine its susceptibility to the current and alternative antimicrobial agents in order to avoid delayed infection control due to ineffective treatment. The core role of antimicrobial susceptibility testing is to answer the question, "Which antimicrobial agents is this pathogen susceptible to?" thereby providing a basis for precise antimicrobial therapy in patients with severe pneumonia complicated by lung abscess, empyema, and septic shock, helping to optimize or adjust the antimicrobial regimen, reduce the risk of resistance, and improve the speed of infection control. For such a critically ill patient, with obvious necrosis of the lesion and a need to stabilize respiratory and circulatory status as quickly as possible, the susceptibility results are directly related to subsequent treatment choices and improvement in prognosis.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Through sputum testing, metagenomic sequencing (NGS), and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, Staphylococcus aureus was rapidly identified as the pathogen.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: 1. Severe pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus) secondary to empyema; 2. Septic shock; 3. Respiratory failure;
diagnostic_basis: Medical history, symptoms, signs, ancillary examinations, and chest drainage examination
Sputum testing, metagenomic sequencing (NGS), and drug susceptibility testing
Pathology report of multiple visceral pleural biopsies

treatment_plan: Actively perform pathogen testing and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and use medications rationally
Noninvasive ventilation, continuous positive-pressure oxygen therapy, and endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation if necessary
Aggressive anti-infective and symptomatic treatment, nutritional supplementation, correction of electrolyte disturbances
Flexible medical thoracoscopy under local anesthesia (aspiration of pus, removal of purulent slough, debridement of necrotic tissue, copious normal saline irrigation)
treatment_response: Before intubation, the patient's SaO2 was 60-80%; after treatment, it was 90-100%.

The patient's condition improved rapidly after surgical intervention: the body temperature began to decrease significantly on the first postoperative day, and on the third day the patient was successfully weaned from mechanical ventilation and switched to low-flow oxygen via face mask to maintain oxygenation.

Repeat blood gas analysis showed oxygen saturation remained stable at 95%, partial pressure of oxygen 80 mmHg, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide 35 mmHg, indicating good recovery of respiratory function.

After 1 week of continued anti-infective treatment, the patient's body temperature returned to normal, and indicators including complete blood count and liver and kidney function all returned to the normal range.
After 1 week of consolidation therapy, the patient recovered and was discharged.
